content_voiceover: This page repeats similar concepts from a past board exam year. The first question asks which statement about treating Philadelphia negative myeloproliferative neoplasms is wrong, and the answer is option B. It claims aspirin at 80 to 100 milligrams daily can be used safely without any complication even when the platelet count exceeds 1500 times 10 to the 9 per liter. That is wrong, because extreme thrombocytosis above roughly 1000 to 1500 raises the risk of acquired von Willebrand syndrome, and aspirin in that setting can worsen bleeding risk, so ristocetin cofactor activity should be checked before assuming aspirin is safe. The other options are all correct, reducing hematocrit below 0.45 in PV lowers vascular events, ruxolitinib improves symptoms and quality of life particularly with myelofibrotic transformation, pegylated interferon alfa can reduce the JAK2 V617F allele burden, and long term hydroxyurea carries a very low leukemogenic risk, similar to phlebotomy alone. The second question on this page repeats the treatment free remission discontinuation criteria question, and again the requirement describing patients who failed first line TKI but achieved deep response on second line therapy as adequate for discontinuation is the incorrect one, this time labeled option C.
keypoints: Extreme thrombocytosis above 1000 to 1500 times 10 to the 9 per liter raises acquired von Willebrand syndrome risk with aspirin
Hematocrit under 0.45 is the target in PV to reduce vascular events, per landmark trial data
Ruxolitinib helps symptoms and quality of life in PV, especially with myelofibrotic transformation
Long term hydroxyurea carries very low leukemogenic risk, comparable to phlebotomy alone
TKI discontinuation candidacy still requires that any prior TKI switch was for intolerance, not treatment failure
keypoint_voiceover: Two recurring board pearls here, do not assume aspirin is automatically safe at extreme platelet counts without checking for acquired von Willebrand syndrome, and TFR discontinuation candidates must have switched TKI for intolerance, never because first line therapy failed.
